## lb2

- `lb2.blurry.h`: Recall from a blurred key
- `lb2.blurry.p`: As in the recall puzzle, but each key is several symbols long and some of them are swapped for others before the question. An exact-match memory would fail as soon as one symbol changes. A sparse distributed memory should degrade slowly, because a blurred key still wakes many of the same slots.
- `lb2.chip.fades`: {h} fades
- `lb2.chip.size`: one size at any length
- `lb2.chip.window`: no window
- `lb2.copy.h`: Copy a run of symbols
- `lb2.copy.p`: A run of random symbols is followed by the same run again, and every symbol of the second run is scored. To copy, a model must step back by one and match by content. Here the transformer leads at the shortest length, and every model falls away as the run grows.
- `lb2.cost.label`: THE COST PER TOKEN
- `lb2.cost.p1`: To go on writing, either model keeps only its memory: {mb} MB at the size we train, whether the text so far is ten tokens or ten thousand. A transformer keeps a cache that grows by one entry with every token, so a longer text costs it more memory and more work for every new token.
- `lb2.cost.p2`: The memory is not free, though. On one GPU the same layers with the memory switched off train at {o} tokens a second; PARTIAL trains at {p} and FULL at {fu}. Most of each model’s time goes to its memory.
- `lb2.cost.title`: One size at any length
- `lb2.fades.f0`: Fade {f}: only the token just before survives, so this head is a one-step look back.
- `lb2.fades.f1`: Fade {f}: a write halves in about {h} tokens, so this head holds the last few words.
- `lb2.fades.f2`: Fade {f}: a write halves in about {h} tokens, so this head holds the last few sentences.
- `lb2.fades.f3`: Fade {f}: nothing fades, so this head holds the whole text, blended together.
- `lb2.fades.label`: THE FADES
- `lb2.fades.p1`: Each layer’s memory has {h} heads, and before every new write each head multiplies what it holds by its own fade. A write made some tokens back counts the fade once for every token since.
- `lb2.fades.p2`: The fades are the same in FULL and in PARTIAL. The think step that follows, the table or the MLP, works on the current token alone and holds no past.
- `lb2.fades.title`: One head for the last token, one that never forgets
- `lb2.not.l1`: One run each, one seed. A gap of a few points between two models is inside what a second seed could move.
- `lb2.not.l2`: Small models on puzzles with their own alphabet, where the noise is easy to tell apart from the keys. A model that wins here may still lose on real text.
- `lb2.not.title`: What the puzzles do not show
- `lb2.puzzles.before`: The puzzles were run before FULL was chosen, so FULL has no puzzle scores; the charts below are PARTIAL’s alone.
- `lb2.puzzles.label`: THE PUZZLES
- `lb2.puzzles.p1`: These puzzles test the memory alone, on small versions of the models: {w} wide and {l} layers, each trained for {s} steps on the puzzle itself. Each sequence holds {n} pairs of a key and a value, and then asks for some of the values back. Guessing gives about {c}% right.
- `lb2.puzzles.title`: The memory puzzles, measured
- `lb2.recall.h`: Recall after a gap
- `lb2.recall.p`: A gap of noise sits between the pairs and the questions. The models trained with gaps of up to {g} tokens, so the longer gaps were never seen in training. PARTIAL answers {a}% right at a gap of {g0} and {b}% at {g1}. With the memory off the answers sit at chance. The transformer answers {ta}% at {g0} and falls to {tb}% at {g1}.
- `lb2.top.go`: how it forgets
- `lb2.top.lede`: Neither model has a window of past tokens to look back over. Each reads only the newest token, and everything earlier lives in a memory of fixed size that the text writes into as it goes. This page shows how that memory forgets, why it costs the same at any length, and what the memory puzzles measured.
- `lb2.top.puzzles`: the puzzles
- `lb2.top.sub`: How far back FULL and PARTIAL reach, and what it costs them.
- `lb2.window.label`: NO WINDOW
- `lb2.window.p1`: A transformer keeps every earlier token and looks straight back at any of them. FULL and PARTIAL keep none of them. Each token writes into the memory and reads from it, and later tokens find what it left there by content, through the address.
- `lb2.window.p2`: The memory is lossy, because many tokens write into the same slots and their values mix. What the model keeps is a blend, not a copy. The fades decide how fast the blend forgets.
- `lb2.window.title`: The past is in the memory, nowhere else

The film shows its weights for the 59 numbers, seen through one frequency: a tangle that closes into a ring, each number taking its own place. Each hidden unit settles on one Fourier frequency while weight decay pulls the memorised answer toward the general rule. Nothing is left out: once the rule is learned, every number has a home on the ring.

- `learning.dyn.taught.muon`: Muon gives every direction a fair step: all 8 directions of a target reach 90% by step 233, the faintest first, while plain gradient descent leaves the faintest behind.
- `learning.dyn.taught.sdm`: In our SDM language model one batch's gradient reaches only the memory rows its reads woke, 3,038 of 65,536 in the first table. That is how it learns, not a gain: at 20M tokens its reads still score the same as no reads (1.668 against 1.662 bits per byte).

- `learning.dyn.taught.tngd`: A settling particle can do the linear algebra of learning: its average position lands within 0.91% of the natural-gradient step, the idea behind thermodynamic natural gradient descent.
- `learning.explain.classic`: The classic route. A second machine learns only the pixels (no labels). Its hidden things' yes-rates become 500 features, and an ordinary logistic regression reads the digit from them. That is how Boltzmann machines were first used on MNIST.
- `learning.explain.coins`: Given the pixels and labels, each hidden thing flips its own coin; given the hidden things, each label does. Doing all hidden then all visible is one exact sweep of the sampler.
- `learning.explain.kinds`: The machine has three kinds of things, each yes or no. 784 pixel things (a pixel is yes when its grey value is at least 128 of 255), ten label things (one per digit), and a layer of hidden things the machine uses however helps it. Every hidden thing pulls on every pixel and every label; nothing else is connected. That shape is a restricted Boltzmann machine.
- `learning.explain.learning`: Learning. Show the machine a digit with its label held on. Let it take one step on its own (settle the hidden things, rebuild the picture, settle the hidden things again). Then move every pull toward what the example did and away from what the machine did by itself.
- `learning.explain.likely`: An arrangement is likely when things agree with their leans and when pulled pairs agree.
- `learning.explain.plain`: The machine is an energy over pixels, labels and hidden things. Learning lowers the energy of real digits with their labels, and reading a digit lets the labels settle against held pixels.
- `learning.explain.reading`: Reading a digit. Hold a new digit's pixels, let the hidden and label things shake, and take the label that is yes most often. That is the settled readout. The exact readout computes, for each of the ten labels, how likely the machine finds that label with these pixels, and takes the best. It draws no coins.
- `learning.explain.rule`: Raise a pull when the examples agree on that pair more often than the machine does after a short settle (contrastive divergence, one step); the last term keeps pulls small. η starts at 0.005 and falls to a tenth over 20 passes.
- `learning.guide.dream.awake`: AWAKE: push the real digit down
- `learning.guide.dream.cap`: The energy over all pictures; lower means more likely. Awake, the valley under a real digit is pushed down; dreaming, the valley the machine wandered into on its own is pushed up, until it is a hill.
- `learning.guide.dream.dream`: a dream
- `learning.guide.dream.dreaming`: DREAMING: push the dream up
- `learning.guide.dream.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 3 · AWAKE AND DREAMING
- `learning.guide.dream.p1`: Learning changes the leans and pulls so that real digits get a low energy. Lowering them alone is not enough, since the machine could make every picture likely. So each step also raises the energy of what the machine imagines on its own.
- `learning.guide.dream.p2`: Awake. The machine is shown a real digit with its label held on. The hidden lights settle against it, and the machine counts how often each pixel and each hidden light agree.
- `learning.guide.dream.p3`: Dreaming. The machine lets go of the digit. From those hidden lights it rebuilds a picture and a label of its own, settles the hidden lights again, and counts the same agreements in its dream.
- `learning.guide.dream.p4`: Each pull then moves by the difference: up where the real digit agreed more than the dream, down where the dream agreed more. Real digits sink into valleys and the dreams are pushed out of them. The method is called contrastive divergence; a dream one step long is CD-1, the rule this page’s machine was trained with.
- `learning.guide.dream.read`: Read it as: the pull between pixel i and hidden light k changes by a small step η times how much more the two agreed awake than in the dream. When the dreams look like the real digits, the difference is zero and learning stops.
- `learning.guide.dream.real`: a real digit
- `learning.guide.dream.title`: Learning: down for real digits, up for dreams
- `learning.guide.filters.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 4 · WHAT A HIDDEN LIGHT COMES TO MEAN
- `learning.guide.filters.p1`: At the start every pull is a little random noise, so a hidden light answers to nothing in particular. As the rounds go by, the pulls from one hidden light to the pixels take on a shape.
- `learning.guide.filters.p2`: The shape is called a filter. The hidden light says yes when ink falls on the pixels it pulls toward lit, and no when ink falls on the pixels it pulls toward dark. Most filters become parts of digits: a bar, a curve, the loop of a 6, the corner of a 7.
- `learning.guide.filters.p3`: Nobody told the machine what a stroke is. Strokes are what let its one-step dreams look like real digits. The INSPECT tool further down draws all 500 filters this machine learned.
- `learning.guide.filters.title`: A hidden light becomes a stroke detector
- `learning.guide.lights.cap`: Pixels on the left, hidden lights in the middle, labels on the right. Every line is a pull. The hidden lights flicker because they are decided again and again.
- `learning.guide.lights.hidden`: hidden
- `learning.guide.lights.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 1 · THE LIGHTS
- `learning.guide.lights.labels`: labels
- `learning.guide.lights.p1`: Picture the machine as a set of lights, each of which says yes or no. The rest of this page calls each light a thing. There are three kinds, and each kind has one job.
- `learning.guide.lights.p2`: The 784 pixel lights hold the picture: a pixel is yes where the ink is. The ten label lights name the digit, one for each of 0 to 9. The hidden lights, 500 of them in the machine on this page, are given no job at all; the machine learns what to use them for.
- `learning.guide.lights.p3`: Every hidden light is joined to every pixel and every label, and no two lights of the same kind are joined. That restriction gives the machine its name, a restricted Boltzmann machine, and it lets all the hidden lights be decided at once.
- `learning.guide.lights.pixels`: pixels
- `learning.guide.lights.title`: A machine made of lights
- `learning.guide.numbers.cap`: Three numbers from this page on one scale from 0 to 100: chance, the plain baseline, and the machine, each the share of the 10,000 test digits read correctly.
- `learning.guide.numbers.chance`: shuffled labels (chance)
- `learning.guide.numbers.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 8 · THE NUMBERS
- `learning.guide.numbers.logistic`: logistic regression
- `learning.guide.numbers.machine`: the machine, settled
- `learning.guide.numbers.p1`: An accuracy is the share of the 10,000 test digits read correctly. The machine never saw those digits while it learned, so the number measures what it learned rather than what it memorised.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p2`: Every result names its readout. Settled means counted from a live settle, coins and all; exact means computed with no coins. The gap between the two is the cost of reading by settling.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p3`: Two fixed points stand beside every result. Logistic regression on the same black and white pixels is the plain baseline a learner should beat. A machine trained on shuffled labels shows chance, about 10 in 100, so a score far above it was not reached by luck.
- `learning.guide.numbers.p4`: A sweep is one look at every hidden and label light. More sweeps give a firmer vote, and the chart under RECORDED · SETTLE TIME shows how fast it firms. A mean of 3 seeds means the machine was trained three times from different random starts and the scores were averaged.
- `learning.guide.numbers.title`: What the numbers on this page mean
- `learning.guide.pair.cap`: Two lights joined by a positive pull, shown in turn in all four arrangements. When they agree the energy is low; when they disagree it is high.
- `learning.guide.pair.energy`: energy
- `learning.guide.pair.high`: disagree: high
- `learning.guide.pair.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 2 · LEANS, PULLS AND THE ENERGY
- `learning.guide.pair.low`: agree: low
- `learning.guide.pair.p1`: Each light has a lean, a number saying which answer it prefers on its own. Each joined pair has a pull, a number saying how much the two want to agree. A positive pull wants them to match; a negative pull wants them to differ.
- `learning.guide.pair.p2`: The energy adds up how unhappy an arrangement is. Every light that goes against its lean adds to it, and every pair that goes against its pull adds to it. The machine finds an arrangement of low energy likely and one of high energy unlikely.
- `learning.guide.pair.pull`: pull
- `learning.guide.pair.read`: Read it as: the energy is minus the leans of the pixels and labels (a), minus the leans of the hidden lights (b), minus the pulls (W) between every hidden and visible pair. The chance of an arrangement falls off exponentially with its energy, and Z only makes all the chances add up to one.
- `learning.guide.pair.title`: Leans, pulls and the energy
- `learning.guide.read.cap`: A held 3. The labels flicker while the hidden lights find their places; then one label keeps saying yes, and its count wins the vote.
- `learning.guide.read.held`: held pixels
- `learning.guide.read.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 5 · READING A DIGIT
- `learning.guide.read.p1`: To read a new digit, the machine holds its pixels on and starts the ten labels at random. Then the two layers take turns: the hidden lights settle against the pixels and the labels, and the labels settle against the hidden lights.
- `learning.guide.read.p2`: At first the labels flicker, because the hidden lights have not agreed yet. Within a few sweeps one label keeps saying yes. The machine counts each label’s yeses over the settle and answers with the one that said yes most often.
- `learning.guide.read.p3`: That answer is the settled readout. The exact readout tosses no coins: it works out how likely each label is with these pixels and takes the best. The two agree on almost every digit.
- `learning.guide.read.title`: Reading is settling with the pixels held
- `learning.guide.read.votes`: votes
- `learning.guide.temp.label`: HOW IT LEARNS · 7 · TEMPERATURE
- `learning.guide.temp.p1`: Each light decides by tossing a weighted coin. Its input, its lean plus the pulls of the lights it is joined to, sets the weight: a strong input makes the coin nearly certain, a weak one leaves it nearly fair.
- `learning.guide.temp.p2`: The temperature divides the input before the toss. Hot, every coin is close to fair and the lights jitter. Cold, every coin follows its input and the lights freeze into the arrangement the pulls favour.
- `learning.guide.temp.p3`: This machine was trained and is read at temperature 1, so its learned pulls already say how sure it should be. The live settle above has a temperature slider: heat the machine and its answer wanders, cool it and the answer locks.
- `learning.guide.temp.read`: Read it as: the chance a light says yes rises from 0 to 1 as its input goes from strongly negative to strongly positive, and the temperature T sets how steep the rise is.
- `learning.guide.temp.title`: What the temperature does

- `lsdm2.differ.p1`: Without the word table, FULL has {a} weights and PARTIAL has {b}, almost the same. PARTIAL’s MLP uses all of its weights for every token. FULL’s table reads {r} rows a layer for each token, so most of its weights sit unused on any one token. A larger table would cost more memory and no more work per token.
- `lsdm2.differ.p2`: Today the dense MLP trains faster. On one GPU, PARTIAL trains at about {p} tokens a second and FULL at about {f}. With the memory switched off the same layers run at {o}, so the memory between tokens is most of the cost of both.

- `lsdm2.not.l2`: The pictures show the steps the code takes. A light stands for a part, not for one weight, and the counts in the captions are the real ones.
- `lsdm2.not.l3`: The memory puzzles on the lookback page were run with small versions of these models, not at the size we train them.
- `lsdm2.not.label`: WHAT WE DO NOT CLAIM

- `lsdm2.read.label`: HOW IT READS
- `lsdm2.read.more`: The address itself, a grid searched from two short lists, is drawn on sdm-unfold.
- `lsdm2.read.p1`: Each token also makes a query. The query picks {k} slots the same way the key did, and the read is the weighted mean of what was written there. A slot nobody wrote reads as nothing. A token reads before it writes, so it only ever sees earlier tokens.
- `lsdm2.read.p2`: Then comes the think step. In FULL, a second query picks {k} of the table’s {s} rows in each head, about {p}% of them, and blends those rows with a softmax. In PARTIAL, the MLP widens the vector to {n} numbers, gates it and narrows it back, and every weight takes part.
- `lsdm2.read.title`: A query, a weighted mean, then the think step
- `lsdm2.step.label`: THE NEXT TOKEN
- `lsdm2.step.more`: In more detail: enfold and unfold, and <a2>how far back the memory reaches</a2>.
- `lsdm2.step.s1`: Enfold: the newest token’s row of the word table becomes a vector of {d} numbers.
- `lsdm2.step.s2`: Each of the {n} layers reads its memory, writes the token into it and adds the read to the vector, then adds its think step.
- `lsdm2.step.s3`: Unfold: the last vector is scored against the same word table, one score for each of the {v} words.
- `lsdm2.step.s4`: The scores become chances and one token is drawn. It becomes the next input, and the memory carries everything that came before.
- `lsdm2.step.title`: How either model writes, one token at a time
- `lsdm2.store.label`: WHAT EACH STORES
- `lsdm2.store.p1`: The memory between tokens is written while the model reads. Each layer has {h} heads, each head has {s} slots, and each slot keeps a running sum of the values written into it and how much was written. It starts empty for every new text, and it holds only what this text has put there.
- `lsdm2.store.p2`: FULL’s table and PARTIAL’s MLP are written by training and then frozen. They hold what the model learned from all of its training text. Reading never changes them.
- `lsdm2.store.title`: A memory for this text, and a store for everything learned
- `lsdm2.top.go`: the two models
- `lsdm2.top.history`: the history
- `lsdm2.top.lede`: Both models are built from sparse distributed memories, and neither has attention. FULL is SDM all the way through. PARTIAL keeps one ordinary part, the MLP. This page shows what each one stores, how it writes and reads, how it picks the next word, and why FULL is the one we take forward.
- `lsdm2.top.sub`: Our two SDM language models, FULL and PARTIAL, taken apart.
- `lsdm2.two.label`: THE TWO MODELS
- `lsdm2.two.p1`: Both models read a text one token at a time, through {n} layers. Every layer does two things. First it writes the token into a memory and reads back what earlier tokens wrote there. That memory is the only way one position in the text learns anything about another. Second, it thinks about the current token on its own.
- `lsdm2.two.p2`: The two models differ only in that second step. In PARTIAL it is an ordinary MLP of {n} neurons, every one of them used for every token. In FULL it is a trained SDM table of {s} rows in each of {h} heads, and each token reads {k} of them.
- `lsdm2.two.title`: One memory between tokens, two ways to think
- `lsdm2.why.behind`: PARTIAL did better on the first test, and FULL goes forward anyway. What we want to learn is how far a model built only from SDMs can go.
- `lsdm2.why.full`: FULL asks a second question: can a sparse trained table do the MLP’s job too? The idea comes from the cerebellum, whose wiring Kanerva’s SDM was first modelled on: for each input only a few cells out of very many fire. If it works, a model can grow its table without growing its work per token.
- `lsdm2.why.label`: WHY WE TRY EACH
- `lsdm2.why.off`: Both are measured against a control: the same layers with the memory switched off, so that nothing at all passes between positions. A model that cannot beat it has learned nothing from its memory.
- `lsdm2.why.partial`: PARTIAL keeps the MLP, which nearly every working language model has. So it asks one new question: does a memory written while reading make a better language model?
- `lsdm2.why.ruling`: FULL goes forward. It becomes the base of the next SDM CHAT. We are trying other shapes of it now, in the shape sweep below, and each winning shape is to be compared with a transformer of the same shape. PARTIAL stops after its first test, where it served as the comparison.
- `lsdm2.why.title`: Two questions, a control, and the one we take forward
- `lsdm2.write.label`: HOW IT WRITES
- `lsdm2.write.p1`: From its vector, each token makes a key, a value and a gate. The key picks the best {k} of a head’s {s} slots. The value is added into those slots, weighted by how well each one matched. The gate scales the whole write between nothing and full strength, so a token that matters little can write weakly.
- `lsdm2.write.p2`: Before each new write, every head fades what it already holds by its own factor: {a}, {b}, {c} and {d}. A head with a fade of {a} keeps only the newest token, so it works as a one-step look back. A head with a fade of {d} never forgets.
- `lsdm2.write.p3`: The table and the MLP take no writes while the model reads. Training changes them, a little after every batch of text.
- `lsdm2.write.title`: A key, a value and a gate

On the {test} held-out test questions the head agrees with the teacher on {agree} of them.
- `magic8.intro.p3`: The head was taught to copy the teacher. The teacher is a small base model and is near chance on the truth (see HOW IT WAS TRAINED), so this is a magic 8 ball, no oracle.

- `memory.dense.label`: MEASURED · DENSE MEMORY
- `memory.dense.p1`: The Hopfield memory above sums its patterns' pulls in pairs. Krotov and Hopfield's dense memory raises each pattern's overlap to a higher power before it votes, which makes the valleys steeper and lets many more of them fit. We measured it on the CPU: at 48 units, recall from 10% noise held 6 patterns with pairs, 76 with the cube, 512 with the fourth power, and at least 8,192 with the exponential.
- `memory.dense.p2`: With the exponential, one update is the read that attention does: the query weighs every stored pattern by a softmax and moves to their average. Its error falls as exp(-beta times separation); the measured slope was -1.018. Lower beta and memories that share parts settle together: twelve memories in three families gave one fixed point below beta 4.0, three family prototypes between 4.6 and 14.7, and all twelve from 24.8.
- `memory.dense.p3`: These are memories of random or drawn patterns read by their own rules, so they show a mechanism, not a result about our SDM language model, whose learned store, every time it trained stably, tied a model without it, up to 2.0 billion tokens. The link is the sharpness: our soft read's cut-off plays the part that beta plays here.
- `memory.dense.pick.dream`: Forty random starts of a Hopfield net, before (left) and after (right) it dreams: a disc ends in a stored memory, a ring in a false one. Hopfield, Feinstein and Palmer let the net settle from noise and gently weaken whatever it settled into; false memories are the ones it falls into most, so they fade first. After 304 dreams 28 starts find a true memory, against 7 before.
- `memory.dense.pick.family`: Twelve memories in three families, drawn on a plane: rings are the memories, discs are where each one settles. Each family shares a part, and the inverse temperature beta works like a zoom: at high beta every memory keeps itself, between 4.6 and 14.7 the members of a family settle together on what they share, and below that all twelve agree on one point. Nothing is lost by agreeing: turn beta up and every memory is back.
- `memory.dense.pick.wells`: The energy of a modern Hopfield net holding two close memories, drawn as contour lines, while beta falls. Two wells become one at beta 6.067 in the run, and 6.014 from a line of algebra: at the midpoint the update has slope beta times sin squared of the half-angle, and the wells part when it reaches one. Two memories near each other can share one home without either being erased.

- `memory.lm.why.label`: WHY MEMORY MAY NOT PAY ON THIS TEST
- `memory.lm.why.p1`: Our model has no context window in the transformer sense. It sees the last {back} tokens exactly, plus {avg} fading averages of everything before them. The slowest average loses half of what it holds in about {half} tokens, so its real reach is about {reach} tokens. The lookback page tells the full story.
- `memory.lm.why.p2`: Guessing the next token of web text is mostly a local job. The last few words carry most of the answer, and a memory of facts from far back has little to add to that score.
- `memory.lm.why.p3`: Our yardstick shares the blind spot. The transformer we compare against trains on windows of {tw} tokens. Neither model has been asked to remember something from long ago.
- `memory.lm.why.p4`: A recall test would ask exactly that: a fact seen once, needed later. Bits per byte averages over every byte, so it can hide a memory that matters on the few bytes where recall counts. We have not run that test yet.
- `memory.lm.why.p5`: One more clue, with memory off: a longer training window helps up to about {w2} tokens ({a} at {w1}, {b} at {w2}), then goes flat ({c} at {w3}) and then worse ({d} at {w4}). Our reading, untested: at window {w1} many positions sit near the start of their example, where the fading averages have not filled yet. Past {w2}, almost every position already has its full lookback. That fits a reach of a few hundred tokens at most.

## paper

- `paper.abstract`: Abstract. “We put the lime in the coconut and shake it all about.” The sentence is exact, and this paper does no more than say so at length, which is to say briefly. The coconut is a set of pulls between things that are each yes or no; the lime is a set of leans upon them; to shake is to let each thing in turn take a side with the odds its neighbours give it. What remains when the shaking has gone on long enough is the Boltzmann distribution. Without the lime the coconut has no up, and a tumble lands as readily in the mirror as in the memory; with it, one valley is chosen.

## privacy

- `privacy.browser.clear`: You can remove all of it at once by clearing this site’s data in your browser’s settings.
- `privacy.browser.groups`: The site keeps a few small things in your browser so that your choices hold on the next page or the next visit. They fall into the groups below. None of them is used for advertising or to follow you across other sites, and none is sent anywhere by default.
- `privacy.browser.label`: IN YOUR BROWSER
- `privacy.browser.memory`: Some things live only in the page’s memory and are gone when you reload: your ADJUST choices on the home hero, the pointer and key timings the contact page records, and the random visit id a rating carries.
- `privacy.browser.title`: What the site keeps in your browser
- `privacy.check.gate`: A score of 0.6 or more sends the message. A lower score does not end anything: a small puzzle opens, you slide a loose piece until it fits its cut-out, and then the message goes. The server draws the puzzle and keeps its answer. It also turns a message away when the hidden field is filled and the score is under 0.2.
- `privacy.check.h`: How the check tells a hand from a script
- `privacy.check.note`: Our own check, used on this contact page only. In the browser it records pointer positions with times and key timings (never which keys), in memory. Pointer: the trace is cut into strokes at pauses and each stroke is measured for straightness, a rise-and-fall speed profile, smooth speed changes, speed spread, sharp turns, hand tremor, the walk exponent (1 for a random walk, exactly 2 for a ruler line, a hand is neither), sample timing, pauses and slowing before clicks. Keyboard: spread of the gaps between keys, key hold times, corrections and Tab moves, so a keyboard or screen-reader user passes without a mouse. Each measure maps to 0..1 and a weighted mean gives the score; the larger of the two paths counts. A hidden field and a minimum time before sending are cheap extras. Only the score and these reasons are sent; the trace is dropped when the page closes.
- `privacy.contact.intro`: The contact form sends a message only when you press send. A quick check that you are a person runs while you are on that page.
- `privacy.contact.label`: THE CONTACT FORM
- `privacy.contact.mail`: The email is delivered by Resend, a mail delivery service, which handles it under its own terms. Its reply address is yours, so an answer comes back to you.
- `privacy.contact.p1`: The pointer check runs in your browser. It keeps pointer positions with their times, and the time of each key press with its kind (a character, a correction, Tab), never which key.
- `privacy.contact.p2`: Sending the form sends your name, your email, your message, the check score, its verdict and its reason lines. It does not send the pointer path or the key timings.
- `privacy.contact.p3`: Nothing else is stored. The contact page sets no cookie and writes nothing to your browser storage, and the recorded movement is gone when you leave the page.
- `privacy.contact.p4`: The message goes by email to our inbox. To limit how many arrive in ten minutes, the server counts recent messages from each network address: in memory, or, where the site has a members database, as a count under a salted hash of the address.
- `privacy.contact.p5`: If the puzzle opens, the page sends the slider position you chose and nothing else about it. The server keeps a used puzzle and a count of missed tries, in memory, for a few minutes.
- `privacy.contact.title`: What the contact form records and sends
- `privacy.feedback.anon`: If you are not signed in, a rating is kept with a salted hash of your network address, never the address itself. The hash lets us limit how fast one network can send ratings. Only our server holds the secret salt it is made with.
- `privacy.feedback.gate`: Before a rating or a note counts, a check in your browser looks at how the pointer moves, how the page scrolls and how long you stay, to tell a person from a script. It runs in memory and sends nothing.
- `privacy.feedback.holds`: A rating holds its time, the set that was playing (its mode, theme, tune, beat and the other settings of the sound), your rating, the track as text and a random visit id that is new on every page load. A note holds your words in place of the rating. Nothing in either names you.
- `privacy.feedback.holds2`: A rating holds its time, the set that was playing (its mode, theme, tune, beat and the other settings of the sound), your rating, the track as text and a random visit id that is new on every page load.
- `privacy.feedback.label`: RATE THE DJ
- `privacy.feedback.member`: If you are signed in, a rating is kept with your account instead. A rating of 4 or 5 is a like: it appears on your LIKED SETS page, where you can play the set again or remove it. The download of your data includes your ratings, and deleting your account deletes them.
- `privacy.feedback.notesnone`: WHAT IS THIS? notes are not sent: they stay in your browser.
- `privacy.feedback.ours`: Your ratings are sent to this site’s server and kept in our database.
- `privacy.feedback.p1b`: The rate marks on the home hero let you rate the sound, and WHAT IS THIS? lets you write a note. Neither needs an account.
- `privacy.feedback.sentlive`: Both are sent to our ratings server, which keeps a salted hash of the sender’s network address, never the address itself.
- `privacy.feedback.sentnone`: This copy of the site sends them nowhere: they stay in your browser.
- `privacy.feedback.title`: Ratings and WHAT IS THIS? notes
- `privacy.feedback.totals`: We read the totals for each set, how many people rated it and how many liked it, to learn which sets people like.
- `privacy.here`: privacy
- `privacy.members.ask`: ASK answers questions about SETTLE and KANERVA. Your question and the last six turns of the conversation go to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through OpenRouter, a model service, which asks only for providers that keep no copy of them and handles them under its own terms. The server records the time of each answer and what it cost against your chat balance, never the question itself.
- `privacy.members.label`: MEMBERS AND ASK
- `privacy.members.limits`: To slow down abuse, the server counts recent requests from each network address and each account under a salted hash rather than the address itself: in memory, or in the members database where the site has one. Clerk applies its own limits to signing in.
- `privacy.members.mail`: Clerk emails you the 6-digit codes that confirm your address, sign you in on a new device and reset a password.
- `privacy.members.p1`: Sign-up and sign-in on the members page are run by Clerk (clerk.com), an account service. Clerk holds your email address, the name you give, your password (as a hash, never the password itself) and your sessions, under its own terms. Its script loads only once you open a page in the members folder. This site keeps your Clerk user id, the day it first saw you, your saved runs and your chat balance with what each answer cost.
- `privacy.members.rights`: From your account page you can download what this site holds about you as one JSON file, change your email and your password, and delete your saved runs, your chat balance and your record here. Deleting your record deletes your Clerk sign-in too, unless that sign-in is shared with another site of ours; then the page tells you it was kept, and we remove it when you write to us.
- `privacy.members.runs`: You can save the models you train in SDMSTUDIO to your account: up to 50 runs and 256 MiB in all. A saved run holds its name, its kind, its record and its weights.
- `privacy.members.store`: The account records and the chat balance are kept in a Postgres database at Neon, and the weights of saved runs in Vercel Blob, private storage that only the site’s server can read or hand you a short link to.
- `privacy.members.title`: Members accounts and the ASK page
- `privacy.other.label`: OTHER PARTS
- `privacy.other.mcp`: settle-mcp runs on your own computer when you install it, and talks only to the program that starts it. It sends nothing to us. Its setup step downloads SETTLE and KANERVA from a source you name, and only when you ask.
- `privacy.other.radiolive`: The DJ system on the home page hero shares its sound settings with other listeners, so you can listen together: THE DJ’s settings, the steering and your loops travel as text, never sound, and each listener shows as a coloured dot with a colour name and nothing else.
- `privacy.other.radionone`: The DJ system on the home page hero can share its sound settings with other listeners, so you can listen together. This copy of the site does not switch that on, so nothing is shared.
- `privacy.other.title`: The DJ system and settle-mcp
- `privacy.rights.ask`: You can ask what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, and ask us to delete it. Most of what this site keeps sits in your own browser, where you can see it and clear it yourself.
- `privacy.rights.changes`: If this policy changes, the change appears on this page with a new date.
- `privacy.rights.children`: The site is not aimed at children. If you believe a child has made a members account, write to us and we will delete it.
- `privacy.rights.complain`: Raise any privacy concern with us first. If we do not resolve it, you can complain to the data protection authority where you live.
- `privacy.rights.label`: YOUR RIGHTS
- `privacy.rights.title`: Children, your rights and changes
- `privacy.sent.analytics`: The site counts its visits with Vercel Web Analytics, from Vercel, which hosts the site. Each time you open a page, your browser sends Vercel one page view: the page’s name with nothing after it, the time, and, on your first page, the site that sent you here. Vercel records with it your rough location (country, region and city), your browser and operating system, and your kind of device. It sets no cookie and keeps nothing in your browser. Vercel tells visitors apart by a hash made from each request and discards it after 24 hours; by its own description the page views are recorded anonymously, not tied to you or to your network address. We see only totals.
- `privacy.sent.fonts`: Every page loads its typefaces from Google Fonts (fonts.googleapis.com and fonts.gstatic.com). So your browser asks Google’s servers for them, and Google sees your network address and your browser’s details, as it would for any web request. Japanese, Chinese and Hindi each add one more Google Fonts request, only when you choose that language. The site sends Google nothing else.
- `privacy.sent.label`: WHAT LEAVES YOUR BROWSER
- `privacy.sent.models`: The models on SDM CHAT, SDMPOEM, SDM WEIRD LITTLE GUY, SDMJEV and SDMSTUDIO run in your browser. Their files come from this site, and what you type to them never leaves the tab.
- `privacy.sent.none`: The site runs no analytics, no advertising and no trackers. Apart from the hero’s YouTube slides, it embeds no video players, and it embeds no social media buttons from other sites. A link to another site, such as YouTube, GitHub or arXiv, takes you there only when you follow it, and that site’s own policy then applies.
- `privacy.sent.noneva`: Beyond those page counts and speed measurements, the site runs no other analytics, no advertising and no trackers. Apart from the hero’s YouTube slides, it embeds no video players, and it embeds no social media buttons from other sites. A link to another site, such as YouTube, GitHub or arXiv, takes you there only when you follow it, and that site’s own policy then applies.
- `privacy.sent.p1`: By default the site sends nothing about you to any server. Your browser fetches the site’s own files from the site: its pages, its pictures, its data and the small models the demos run.
- `privacy.sent.p1va`: Apart from the page counts and the speed measurements below, the site sends nothing about you to any server. Your browser fetches the site’s own files from the site: its pages, its pictures, its data and the small models the demos run.
- `privacy.sent.speed`: The site also measures how quickly its pages load and answer, with Vercel Speed Insights, from Vercel. On each page load your browser times a few moments (when the first text and the largest picture appear, how much the layout jumps, how quickly the page answers a click or a key, and how soon the server answered) and sends those timings to Vercel with the page’s name with nothing after it, a short description of the part of the page a timing refers to, your kind of connection (such as 4g), your browser, operating system and kind of device, and your country. It sets no cookie and keeps nothing in your browser. By Vercel’s own description the timings are recorded anonymously and cannot be used to follow a visit from page to page or to identify you. We see only totals.
- `privacy.sent.title`: What leaves your browser, and who sees it
- `privacy.sent.youtube`: The home hero can show a YouTube video as one of its slides. Nothing is fetched from YouTube until a video slide is about to show. Then your browser loads YouTube’s player from www.youtube-nocookie.com, YouTube’s privacy-enhanced address, and the video and its pictures from YouTube’s servers (i.ytimg.com, yt3.ggpht.com and googlevideo.com). YouTube sees your network address, your browser’s details and what you do in its player, under Google’s privacy policy. The site does not load YouTube’s player script from www.youtube.com, and sends YouTube nothing else.

- `puzzles.nonohow.p1b`: The first way to write a start is one thing per possible start, with exactly one of them yes. Moving a run one cell then takes two flips, the old start off and the new one on, and the step between them costs energy, so the cooling machine freezes with runs in the wrong places.
- `puzzles.nonohow.p2`: The domain wall writes a start as a row of "past here" bits that read 1 1 0 0 0: the start is where the ones stop. Moving a run one cell is one flip, and every rule stays a sum over pairs. On the survey's 50 seeds the 10x10 duck went from 0 of 50 solved to 50 of 50 at the same 4,000 sweeps.
- `puzzles.quantum.label`: QUANTUM COUSINS
- `puzzles.quantum.p1`: A max-cut puzzle is an energy, so it can be handed to more than one kind of machine. We wrote one max-cut on 10 nodes and 15 edges as SETTLE pulls and solved it four ways in a seeded simulation: SETTLE's own Gibbs anneal, sixteen copies of the p-bits tied together along imaginary time (simulated quantum annealing), quantum annealing by Schrödinger's equation, and QAOA, a quantum circuit built in layers.
- `puzzles.quantum.p2`: Given enough effort, all four reached the best cut, 13 of the 15 edges: quantum annealing with probability 0.999 over the longest time tried, QAOA with 0.987 at twelve layers, the Gibbs anneal with 0.86 in 64 sweeps, and the sixteen copies with 0.64 in 64 sweeps. A guess would hit it with probability 0.002.
- `puzzles.quantum.p3`: The four efforts are in four different units, measured on a laptop that simulates every quantum amplitude, so the numbers say that each road works on this small puzzle, not that one is faster. The copies of p-bits are ordinary p-bits, so a SETTLE program could write them; what no network of p-bits can do is a Bell test, and that is the line between the two families.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.landscape`: On the left, the expected energy of a one-layer quantum circuit over its two angles, the best pair ringed; on the right, the puzzle it solves, split so that 13 of its 15 edges join opposite sides. An ordinary optimiser walks the landscape to find the angles, so the classical machine and the quantum one share the work.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.lz`: Each frame sweeps one spin through an avoided crossing, more slowly than the last, and the line traces its energy. Fast, it is left on its old level; slow, it follows the lower level all the way, as Landau and Zener's formula says. This is why annealing, quantum or SETTLE's own, is done gently: given time, the state keeps pace with its guide.
- `puzzles.quantum.pick.qaoa`: Each frame adds one layer of a quantum circuit to a 10-node max-cut, and the bars show how likely each cut is. A layer is a phase set by the puzzle's own energy, then a gentle mix; with twelve layers 0.987 of the probability rests on the best cut. A puzzle whose pulls cannot all be kept finds the split that keeps the most of them.

- `relax.dyn.lede`: A settle is many small parts, each following its own rule, ending in one shared state. Physics has studied this kind of agreement for a long time. We ran five small experiments on it and made ten short films about it for the home page; three are below.
- `relax.dyn.p1`: Oscillators with different natural rates stay apart until their coupling passes a critical value, then gather into one rhythm. Above that point the share in step follows a known law (Ott and Antonsen) to within {gap}.
- `relax.dyn.p2`: A ring of cells that each see only a few neighbours never agrees under a plain majority vote ({maj} percent of rings): its borders freeze. The GKL rule moves the borders until they meet, and brings the whole ring to the right answer {gkl} percent of the time.
- `relax.dyn.p3`: A network of oscillators that stores six patterns as phases recalled them {none} percent of the time on its own, and {pull} percent once each phase was gently pulled toward 0 or pi. That pull is what makes an oscillator network an Ising machine, and the machine found the calmest arrangement {fast} percent of the time when the pull rose fast and {slow} percent when it rose slowly, as a settle does when it cools slowly.
- `relax.dyn.title`: How many parts come to agree
- `relax.dyn.why.fern`: Two different starts, the words you and me, are both mapped again and again by the same four shrinking maps. Each step brings them closer, and both end as one fern: whatever you begin as, the same shape takes you in.
- `relax.dyn.why.kuramoto`: Oscillators with different natural rates sit on a circle at their phases. As the coupling rises past a critical value they stop drifting apart and gather into one rhythm, and the arrow, the share in step, grows along the dotted law. It is the simplest case of many parts settling into one shared state.
- `relax.dyn.why.memory`: Each cell is an oscillator; a lit block is in phase with a stored arch. From a third of the arch, the coupling pulls the rest into place until the whole pattern returns, as an SDM read completes a word from part of it. It needed a gentle pull toward 0 or pi to work.

- `relax.script.ask.m.2`: The live class asks the lights the pose wants off, in the row beside the held band and in a row far from it, and counts how often each says yes over the stretch's sweeps.
- `relax.script.ask.m.3`: An asked answer carries sampling noise that shrinks with more sweeps; the exact answer is shown beside the live one for the weather model.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.1`: Last stretch, and it's a QUESTION. You don't ask a class "are you tired?" ONCE. You watch them for a whole song and you COUNT.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.2`: How many counts was that light on? Out of how many? THAT'S your answer. Not yes, not no, honey: HOW OFTEN.
- `relax.script.ask.rich.3`: The row next to the held ones says yes more often than the row way over there. Nobody told them to. They felt it.

- `relax.script.cooldown.dhh.1`: I like a slow cool-down. Fewer surprises at the end.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.1`: The live class cools geometrically from T = {hot} to {calm} over {frames} sweeps, the same ratio every sweep. The home room does the same over about eight seconds.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.2`: settle-rs anneal: T(t) = 10 T x 0.005t/(S-1). "The core anneal cools from 10T to T/20 and keeps the calmest arrangement visited; the range is fixed at 200x."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.3`: Slow cool-downs solve more. 4x4 sudoku, share of 50 anneals that found a valid grid: 28% at 100 sweeps, 88% at 500, 100% at 2,000; random guessing 0%. 9x9 easy: 4% / 32% / 94% at 2,000 / 10,000 / 50,000 sweeps.
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.4`: For decoding codes, the schedule itself is the lever: "What seems to matter is the schedule of the effective odd-check price: soft while hot, hard while cold."
- `relax.script.cooldown.m.5`: In this little class the picture is the only valley, so dropping the heat at once also settles. A slow cool-down pays where there are many valleys, as in sudoku.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.1`: Okay. Okay, babies. Now we come down. Not all at once! You never stop a class dead, you'll CRASH. We bring the heat down a little... and a little... and a little. Every count a bit cooler than the one before.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.2`: Three... two and a half... two... one and a half... Let the picture come up out of the noise. Don't grab it. Let it come to you, honey.
- `relax.script.cooldown.rich.3`: You know why I take my time here? Because the people who rush the cool-down end up in the wrong position and they STAY there. The slow ones find the right one. Every time I have ever watched.
- `relax.script.cooldown.term`: annealing

- `relax.script.relax.m.1`: Temperature T = {calm}, beta = {b}. The same fully agreeing light now says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.relax.m.2`: Overlap q = (1/n) sum of ti si: +1 is the picture exactly, -1 its mirror, 0 unrelated. It is the live overlap percentage.
- `relax.script.relax.m.3`: A valley is an arrangement where every single flip costs energy: dEi = 2 si (hi + sumj Jij sj) > 0 for every i.
- `relax.script.relax.m.4`: Settled is not frozen. The machine keeps sampling; a light still flips now and then, and that is what the next stretch reads.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.1`: ...and here we are. Temperature under a half. Nobody's pushing anybody.
- `relax.script.relax.rich.2`: Every light is doing what its lean says and what its neighbours say, and for once they all say the SAME thing, so it just... stays. Look at the two of us, babies. Nobody switched those lights on by hand. You settled into it.

- `relax.script.warmup.rich.1`: OKAY BABIES, ON YOUR FEET!! Nobody knows the routine yet and THAT IS FINE, honey!! Every one of you is a little light going on, off, on, off, like a coin in a tumble dryer!! Flip! Flop! Flip!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.2`: And listen to me, sweetheart: I do NOT care where you start. Start on, start off, start in the wrong corner of the room. One good sweep and your body forgets it anyway!!
- `relax.script.warmup.rich.3`: And the first few reps DON'T COUNT!! We are loosening up!! Nobody is keeping score in the warm-up, not even me, and I keep score of EVERYTHING!!

- `relax.script.workout.dhh.1`: Lean 0.9, pull 0.3. Sensible defaults, Richard. I would not change them.
- `relax.script.workout.m.1`: Temperature T = {T}, so beta = 1/T = {b}. The home room's hot phase uses the same {T}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.2`: The update rule: P(si = yes) = (1 + tanh(beta Ii)) / 2, with Ii = hi + J times the sum of the neighbours. Lean h = {lean} toward the picture, pull J = {pull} to four neighbours.
- `relax.script.workout.m.3`: One sweep updates every free light once, in a fresh random order. That is exact Gibbs sampling.
- `relax.script.workout.m.4`: A light whose lean and all four neighbours agree has input {agree}; at T {T} it says yes with chance {p}.
- `relax.script.workout.m.5`: Counting reps: with no pulls, each doubling of sweeps buys 3.01 dB. Measured on the Muybridge horse, 150x100: 15.60 / 18.59 / 21.68 / 24.72 / 27.71 dB at 5 / 10 / 20 / 40 / 80 sweeps.
- `relax.script.workout.m.6`: Form check: the film grid is stable only while J z (1 - m2) < 1; with z = 4, that is J < 0.25 at m = 0. Above it the grid flipped to its mirror image, scoring 1.9 to 4.1 dB.
- `relax.script.workout.rich.1`: NOW WE MOVE!! Temperature THREE, babies!! AND ONE, two, three, four, five, six, seven, EIGHT!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.2`: Every light gets two voices in its ear: its own lean, "I think I belong in the picture," and its four NEIGHBOURS, "come with us, honey!" At this heat the voices are small and the jiggle is BIG. Do you see the two of us in there? A little? A LITTLE!! That's a workout!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.3`: Count your reps!! Every time you DOUBLE the reps you get three more decibels of picture. Three! Every time! I have never had a class that consistent in my LIFE!!
- `relax.script.workout.rich.4`: And form check, sweetheart: hold your neighbour's hand, don't CRUSH it!! Pull too hard and the whole row flips into the MIRROR, everybody doing the move backwards, very committed, very wrong!!
- `relax.script.workout.term`: sweeps at T = {T}

- `repo.kanerva.para`: KANERVA is a Sparse Distributed Memory toolbox, and it stands alone: its own kanerva command and its own .kanerva program files. You write long patterns of bits into a few thousand hard locations, each pattern spread over the locations whose addresses lie near it. Then you read one back from a read-address, a copy with some of its bits flipped. The nearby locations vote bit by bit, and the stored pattern comes back. It is named for Pentti Kanerva, who described the memory in 1988. SETTLE mounts its sdm family as a plug-in.

- `repo.settle.para`: SETTLE is a small language for settling machines. You name a few yes-or-no things, say how much each one leans toward yes and how much pairs of them pull toward agreeing, then let the machine settle: every thing keeps flipping like a weighted coin until the whole arrangement calms down. You ask a question by counting how often a thing came up yes. The same few words answer probability questions, clean up pictures, recall memories, solve puzzles and learn from examples.

It lays a grid of lights over the canvas, each one a p-bit that leans toward your picture and is pulled by its four neighbours, and it cools the grid from noise into the picture, then keeps it alive. SettleText takes your words and your font and renders them as a grid of neon lights that comes out of noise, keeps flickering, and shimmers on its own clock. SettleImage does the same for a picture, by brightness, with a dither for photos and the picture’s own colours per light if you want them. SettleVector takes an SVG, by ink. - `sdmexplore.ex.s1.p`: Everything the memory stores or reads is a pattern of bits, here the {n} bits of :cat, drawn as lights: lit for +1, dark for -1. Kanerva’s own examples use a thousand or ten thousand bits. A thousand-bit word has 2 to the power 1,000 possible values, far too many for a memory to keep one location for each.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s1.title`: A word is a long row of bits
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.p`: An ordinary memory has one location for every address. This one has {M} hard locations. Each has a random {n}-bit address, chosen once and kept, and a row of {n} bit-counters that start at zero. The stars are the three stored patterns; each dot is one hard location, drawn near the patterns its address resembles.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s2.title`: The memory builds a few hard locations, at random addresses, and never moves them
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.p`: No hard location has exactly the word’s address. So the word wakes every hard location within the activation radius, {r} bits here, and is added to their bit-counters: +1 where the word has a lit bit, -1 where it has a dark one. Writing :cat woke {k} of the {M}; the other patterns went to other hard locations.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s3.title`: A write spreads the word over the hard locations near it
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.p`: Give the memory an address. The hard locations within {r} bits of it wake, their rows of bit-counters are added up bit by bit, and each bit of the answer is the sign of its column. Shown: the {k} rows woken by a noisy copy of :cat (rose +, indigo -), the column sums, and the answer underneath.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s4.title`: A read lets the nearby hard locations vote
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.p`: That copy of :cat had {flipped} of {n} bits flipped. It woke {shared} of the {k} hard locations :cat was written to, and their votes outweighed the rest: one read left {off} bits wrong, and reading again from each answer reached :cat in {rounds} reads and then stopped changing. The chart counts the bits that differ from :cat after each read. An address far from every stored word wakes hard locations that agree on nothing, and the answer is noise, which is the memory’s way of saying it does not know.
- `sdmexplore.ex.s5.title`: A noisy address still finds the word, read by read

- `sdmexplore.page.cap.line`: The critical-distance is a second prediction, and it is not settled. At Kanerva’s point (1,000 bits, a million hard locations, radius 451, 10,000 words) KANERVA’s S-map gives 165 bits, Bricken and Pehlevan report 188, and a real store measured 204.3. Nobody has explained the gap. Radius 451 activates 1,072 of the million hard locations; Kanerva 1993’s own sample memory uses radius 447, which activates 445.
- `sdmexplore.page.cap.p`: Kanerva 1993 gives the capacity as a share of the hard locations, where φ is the chance a stored bit is read back right from its exact address. At φ = 0.999 it is 0.105 words per hard location as the memory grows without end, and 0.096 for his million-location sample memory. KANERVA’s theory module reproduces both numbers in its tests. A noisy address holds fewer.
- `sdmexplore.page.cap.title`: How much a memory holds, by Kanerva’s theory

- `sdmexplore.page.exp.label`: EXPERIMENTS · SETTLE × KANERVA
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.p`: Each one runs the memory here and sets its result beside a recorded or sealed number. They show where the memory holds, where it melts, and what a key or a refusal rule does to a read.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.title`: Experiments you can run in this tab
- `sdmexplore.page.exp.track`: Experiment 2 sets the S-map’s prediction beside the count. The plain map is optimistic once the address-noise reaches 30%: at a million hard locations it predicted 1,648 words at 30% noise where 700 were measured. KANERVA’s TRACK prediction follows the measured recall (the KANERVA page shows both).
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.p`: Start from a 10% noisy address, read 30 times at one temperature, and count how many of the last ten reads sit on the pattern. A tied bit (sum exactly 0) is a fair coin at any heat. With a self-pull of 0.5 it leans to keep its value, which is the T = 0 tie rule written as a lean.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp1.title`: The memory melts as it warms
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.p`: Kanerva's size: 256 bits, 2,000 locations, radius 112. Random patterns are written one at a time. After each, 48 stored patterns are read back from noisy addresses. The S-map (Bricken and Pehlevan's signal-to-noise map, ported from KANERVA) predicts the largest count that still converges. We recorded where recall first fell under 90%.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp2.title`: How many patterns fit, against the S-map's prediction
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.p`: In the small memory almost every address falls into some stored pattern, so landing on one proves nothing. The travel rule asks how far the answer moved from its address. A stored pattern within h bits of a random address is unlikely, so an answer farther than h is refused.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp3.title`: Refusing an address that was never stored
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.p`: settle-rs keeps the bit-counters as pulls between 64 hard location things and 32 data things. Settle that model and each hard location is itself a p-bit: it switches on when the data agree with what it holds, and the data take the vote of the hard locations that are on. At temperature 0 this is the {via} read.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp4.title`: The hard locations as settling p-bits
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.p`: A soft SDM lets a hard location fire with a chance that falls with its distance d. That chance is the p-bit rule with lean t minus d at temperature 2w. As the softness grows the edge of the ball blurs, and t is re-fitted so the expected number of active locations stays the same. At the soft end the read approaches attention.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp5.title`: In a soft SDM a hard location is a p-bit leaning by its distance
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.p`: A key names a turn of the cube: a sign flip on every bit and a shuffle of positions. The note, its length byte and a padding of +1s are turned and stored; nothing else of the text is kept. The key's address is the turned all-+1 list, which agrees with the note on the padding only. So a short note is found, and a long one leaves the address too far away for an SDM's narrow basins.
- `sdmexplore.page.exp6.title`: A note only its key can find

- `sdmexplore.page.machine.p`: Pick a start on the left: a stored pattern with some of its bits flipped (a noisy address), a word that was never stored, or pure noise. The hard locations within 12 bits of the address wake and vote, and the answer appears on the right. Press RUN and the answer becomes the next address, until the read gives back what it was given. Press an address bit to flip it, or hold it.
- `sdmexplore.page.machine.title`: Pick an address and watch it answer

- `sdmexplore.page.output.p`: Look at the last two lines: an address that was never written (:zebra) and pure noise both come back as :cat. In a memory this small the basins cover most of the cube. Experiment 3 refuses such reads.

- `sdmexplore.page.prog.title`: Write it in SETTLE
- `sdmexplore.page.program.line`: The addresses come from the memory's name and seed (FNV-1a of {name}), each pattern from its name, and each noisy address from its seed. So the program and the machine hold the same 64 addresses, the same patterns and the same bit-counters.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.p`: Sixteen lines of SETTLE build the machine. The program calls the read-address {ra}; Kanerva calls it the retrieval address, or the retrieval cue. {an} flips a tenth of its bits.
- `sdmexplore.page.program.title`: The same memory, as a SETTLE program
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.line`: A write adds the pattern, as +1 and -1, to every woken hard-location's bit-counters. A read adds the woken bit-counters bit by bit; a sum of exactly 0 keeps the bit it had.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.p`: THE VOTE panel under the diagram shows it. Each woken hard-location is a row of 32 bit-counters, rose for positive and indigo for negative. The sums are the bars; the sign of each bar is one bit of the answer. The amber ring marks a tie.
- `sdmexplore.page.vote.title`: Add the bit-counters, keep the sign
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.line`: The dashed circle in the diagram is this set. Move the address and the circle keeps its size while the hard locations slide in and out of it.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.p`: The distance between two words is the number of bits where they differ. A hard location wakes when its address is within the activation radius. With 64 random addresses and activation radius 12, about five wake for any address.
- `sdmexplore.page.wake.title`: Every hard location within 12 bits wakes
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.line`: Given the address, the 32 bits are independent, so the chance that one read lands on a pattern is the product of the 32 chances. The diagram prints it and counts 400 reads beside it. This read picks hard locations by address and votes with bit-counters, so it is not a settle of one energy. Experiment 4 is.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.p`: Turn the temperature up in the diagram. At T = 0 a bit takes the sign of its sum. Warm, it is a weighted coin, SETTLE's p-bit: a big sum still almost always wins, a small sum is a near toss-up. The memory holds its pattern when warm and melts when hot.
- `sdmexplore.page.warm.title`: Warm, each bit becomes a p-bit
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l1`: Two random codes of 40 bits in 2,048 share 0.78 bits on average; in 200,000 draws none shared more than 7.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l2`: Keep 3 of the 40 bits and the fragment still shares more with its code than the best of 10,000 strangers does.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l3`: One union of codes held to one false match in a billion fits 3 codes at 4 active bits, 47 at 28 and 14 at 400: there is a best sparsity.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.l4`: Read as a sparse code, our SDM language model's first read wakes 32 of 65,536 locations a token and a quarter of all wakes go to 32 locations. That describes the code, not its worth: every time the trained reads trained stably, they tied a model with no reads, up to 2.0 billion tokens.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.label`: SPARSE CODES · WHAT MANY BITS AGREE ON
- `sdmexplore.sparse.p`: The memory above reads with dense addresses. A sparse distributed representation uses very few active bits, 40 of 2,048 here, and two codes are alike when they share bits. Three small experiments, run in a few minutes on a laptop, show why so few bits are enough.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick1.p`: Four columns each touch a different part of one object among 1,000. Alone, each keeps 322 to 350 objects that fit what it felt. They vote, and after two touches all four hold the same one. Pooled evidence settles a question no single column could settle so soon.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick1.title`: Columns that agree
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick2.p`: Each of a code's 40 bits is moved at random with a growing probability. A match needs only 20 shared bits, so the code still knows itself 56.55% of the time when half its bits are moved, just as the binomial law says, while a stranger matches with probability 2.5e-26. A sparse code forgives a great deal and still refuses a stranger.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick2.title`: Noise forgiven
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick3.p`: A spatial pooler of 64 columns learns from random bars, 4 winners for each input. Boosting raises a quiet column and lowers a busy one, so the busiest wins 1.30 times its fair share instead of 2.32. Its fields sharpen into single bars, 53 of 64 clean, and all 16 bars are taken.
- `sdmexplore.sparse.pick3.title`: Each finds its own part

## sdmintro

- `sdmintro.p`: A sparse distributed memory is Kanerva’s memory for long words of bits. It has a few thousand hard locations, each at a fixed random address with a row of bit-counters. A write adds a word to the hard locations near its address. A read wakes the hard locations near the read-address and lets their bit-counters vote, bit by bit, so a noisy address still finds the stored word. The five-step explainer, with pictures, is at the top of SDM EXPLORE.

- `sdmm.law.p1`: Every model on this page is built from one part: a sparse distributed memory, Kanerva’s store of hard locations read by an address. The only step that lets one position in the text affect another is an SDM read or write. There is no attention, no softmax over the window, no transformer anywhere in a model we score. The transformer below is a yardstick only, there to say how far the SDM trails.

A residual stack where every layer adds a run-time Kanerva memory, written and read as the text goes by, and no attention anywhere.

- `sdmm.shape.mixer.w`: each token writes
- `sdmm.shape.mixer.why`: If a trained store adds nothing, let the text itself write into the memory as it is read. Each token writes a value into the locations its address wakes; later tokens read what earlier ones wrote. That is attention’s job, by content, at a fixed cost per token at any length.

- `sdmtruth.score.bracket`: Bracketed or unbracketed. A sweep changes one setting. If the best score sits inside the range tried, the sweep is BRACKETED and the best value is found. If the best is at the edge, it is UNBRACKETED, and the next sweep tries further out.
- `sdmtruth.score.label`: HOW WE SCORE
- `sdmtruth.score.line`: The score is how many bits, on average, the model needs to predict each byte of text it has never seen. Lower is better.
- `sdmtruth.score.noise`: The noise rule. The same setting run on two machines scores up to about {n} apart. So a difference smaller than {n} is not called a win; it is rerun on more data first.
- `sdmtruth.score.p1`: Every run is scored on the same held-out test set from FineWeb-Edu: {tokens} tokens, {bytes} bytes, never used in training. A guess spread evenly over all {vals} byte values would cost {eight} bits a byte. Because the score counts bytes rather than tokens, models with different vocabularies can be compared.
- `sdmtruth.score.tech`: bits per byte = (the sum over the test tokens of -ln p(token)) / (ln 2 × the test bytes). The best run averages {nats} nats per token over {tokens} tokens and {bytes} bytes, which gives {bpb}.
- `sdmtruth.score.title`: Bits per byte, on text the model has never seen
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.avg`: {n} fading
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.back`: {n} past tokens
- `sdmtruth.stack.f.pair`: pair
- `sdmtruth.stack.head`: norm, then the head
- `sdmtruth.stack.hop`: one hop
- `sdmtruth.stack.hopn`: hop {n} of {total}
- `sdmtruth.stack.look`: LOOK UP
- `sdmtruth.stack.look.sub`: wake {k} of {m}
- `sdmtruth.stack.look.sub2`: add what they hold
- `sdmtruth.stack.map`: one linear map to width d
- `sdmtruth.stack.mlp`: small MLP
- `sdmtruth.stack.mlp.sub`: SwiGLU, its own weights
- `sdmtruth.stack.next`: the next token
- `sdmtruth.stack.nolook`: no look-up
- `sdmtruth.stack.nolook.sub`: the drawers are not there
- `sdmtruth.stack.off.desc`: The same stack with the LOOK UP taken out: each hop is only the small MLP. Everything else is the same.
- `sdmtruth.stack.off.title`: Memory off
- `sdmtruth.stack.on.desc`: Read from the bottom up: the text so far becomes 14 feature vectors, one linear map joins them, then a hop repeated {hops} times. In each hop a LOOK UP wakes about {k} of {m} learned drawers and adds what they hold, then a small MLP adds its part. The head picks the next token.
- `sdmtruth.stack.on.title`: Memory on
- `sdmtruth.stack.text`: the text so far
- `sdmtruth.stack.times`: × {n}
- `sdmtruth.tech.cost`: A measured limit: the memory-on path keeps one store-sized buffer per hop ({m} by 1,024 float32 at width 1,024, {mb} MB), so memory on at {hops} hops did not fit a {gb} GB RTX 5090.
- `sdmtruth.tech.features`: Features: the embeddings of the last {back} tokens (t to t-7), {avg} causal moving averages of every earlier embedding (decays 0.5, 0.8, 0.9, 0.97, 0.99) and {pairs} element-wise product of the embeddings of t and t-1. Each is RMS-normalised; the {n} vectors are joined and one linear map takes them to the working width d. The input table is untied; the output head has its own table.
- `sdmtruth.tech.hop`: A hop: x ← x + read(x) when memory is on, then x ← x + SwiGLU(x). After the last hop, an RMS norm and the head. There is no attention: positions meet only through the fixed features, over a window of {w} tokens.
- `sdmtruth.tech.read`: The read is a product-key memory (Lample et al., 2019). A query of 256 numbers, batch-normalised, splits in half; each half scores 256 sub-keys, so a drawer (i, j) of the 256 by 256 grid scores s1[i] + s2[j]. The top 64 drawers are found exactly, each is weighed by sigmoid((s - θ) / 0.25) with θ the {k}nd best score, and their value rows are summed with gain 1/{k}. The values start at zero, so at step one memory on equals memory off.
- `sdmtruth.tech.share`: With --share-store, one shelf of {m} drawers is read by every hop; the 2.0B memory-on twin runs that way. Without it, each hop has a shelf of its own.

- `surprise.bits.label`: SURPRISE · IN BITS
- `surprise.bits.p1`: Surprise has a unit. A sight the model gave probability p costs -log2 p bits: one bit for a fair coin, about ten for a one-in-a-thousand sight. The agent above adds this up over its 42 sense bits every step. The average surprise is the entropy, and it is also the length an ideal coder would write, which is why our SDM language model is scored in bits per byte of text it has not seen.
- `surprise.bits.p2`: A learner that reads the first 60,001 bytes of Pride and Prejudice once, paying -log2 p for each byte before counting it, shows the score in motion: a letter model of order 3 ends at 2.743 bits per byte, between gzip (2.970) and bz2 (2.481).
- `surprise.bits.p3`: Settling can also take back surprise that noise put in. We sent a code through a channel that flips 10% of its bits and let p-bits running SETTLE’s own rule read it back. Held at the temperature that matches the noise, their averaged read left 0.0499 of the bits wrong (from 0.1032), as good as belief propagation (0.0490); the same machine cooled to one state left 0.0601.
- `surprise.bits.p4`: A memory can be counted the same way. A Kanerva SDM that hands back each stored bit right or wrong is itself a noisy channel, and the bits it returns rise toward a ceiling as it fills: at most 0.327 bits a counter with 500 hard-locations. Written so that each pattern is its own address, the same memory reads an address it was never given back as itself, so its bits must be counted beside that control.
- `surprise.bits.p5`: These are seeded simulations on a laptop. The decoder is not fast, the code is far from Shannon’s limit, and none of it is a claim about our language model’s store. The three pictures below come from that experiment, drawn live.
- `surprise.bits.pick.decode`: Two linked rings arrive with 77 of their 1,344 bits flipped by a noisy channel. Each bit is a p-bit, coupled to the others by the code the rings were sent in; held at the temperature that matches the noise, their running average settles, and 15 wrong bits remain after 48 sweeps. The decoder is exactly as unsure as the channel was noisy, and it trusts the average of many gentle guesses over one cold verdict.
- `surprise.bits.pick.perfect`: Sixteen flowers: each is a codeword of the Hamming(7,4) code at the centre, with the seven words one bit away as petals; beside them, the Fano plane, whose lines are the code’s words of weight 3. The sixteen balls of eight words cover all 128 words of seven bits with no overlap, so every word has exactly one home and any single flipped bit is forgiven.
- `surprise.bits.pick.sdm`: A Kanerva memory of 2,000 hard-locations is given more pairs to hold, from 1 to 7,500, and one stored ring is read back each time. The ring blurs until 95 of its 256 bits are wrong, yet the information the memory returns climbs to about 96,000 bits. Each memory is held a little less sharply so that many more can be held at all.

- `surprise.control.note`: These numbers are live, from the model and the step on screen now. In LEARNING mode the leans and pulls move, so ln Z moves too.
- `surprise.control.p1`: The agent's control is SETTLE-based. Its model is a settling machine: a chain Ising model (a Boltzmann machine whose links form a chain) over the {n} p-bits it senses, with a lean on every bit and pulls between linked bits. Because the links form a chain, ln Z is summed exactly by a transfer matrix, so the surprise of any observation, −ln p(o) = E(o) + ln Z, is exact. To act, the agent steps an imagined copy of the game forward under each of {plans} plans of {horizon} steps, scores every predicted observation by its surprise under the machine, and takes the first move of the plan with the lowest total. Surprise here means how unlikely a sight is under a model fitted to calm wandering: an enemy in view, a hit, a bump or the alarm all make it rise.
- `surprise.control.p2`: It is not SDM. A sparse distributed memory stores patterns at random hard addresses and recalls them by Hamming distance; this agent has no hard locations, no addresses, no counters and no recall. Nothing here uses the Kanerva memory. The settle-drawn picture is SETTLE too: the same p-bit rule, run on the picture’s lights.

Nothing here is saved; reloading starts again. The share of one core is the frame time times the frame rate plus the planning time times the step rate. The game stops while the view is off screen.
- `surprise.controls.help.picture`: EVERY FRAME A SETTLE: every frame the raycaster draws a small picture, and a grid of p-bits takes a few sweeps of the SETTLE rule toward it. NEON BY CLASS: each light shines in a neon chosen by what its pixel shows (sky, sun, cloud, skyline, wall, neon trim, floor, enemy, rain), four tones per class from dark to bright. THE PIXEL'S OWN: each light shines in its pixel's colour. THREE: three grids (red, green, blue) settle each colour on its own. SOFT READ draws each light's running average; RAW BITS draws every light fully on or off. A DAY LASTS sets the length of the day; HOLD stops the sky at the time of day chosen. WEATHER: CYCLE brings rain and night sparks on their own clocks.
- `surprise.controls.help.truetime`: TRUE TIME SETTLE: the game films a frame on a fixed grid and keeps the last {ring}; the settle works toward the frame it was given as fast as this machine allows, and once the lights that frame asked to change agree with it to the threshold, it takes the frame the game is at now. The strip under the view marks each filmed frame SHOWN, SKIPPED, NOW (being settled toward) or FILMED (waiting its turn). MACHINE SPEED: 60 or 15 SWEEPS/S hold the settle to that rate, to show what a slower machine does; the game keeps its time either way.

All of them follow fixed rules with no learning, and the agent's imagined copies of the world run the same rules. - `surprise.fep.choice`: Plans are chosen with probability falling with their expected free energy; γ, the precision, sets how strongly. E(π) is a prior over plans, which in active inference carries habits.
- `surprise.fep.expected`: Expected free energy of a plan π: how far the outcomes the plan is predicted to bring are from the preferred outcomes p̃ (risk), plus how uncertain those outcomes are (ambiguity).
- `surprise.fep.free`: Free energy is surprise plus how far the beliefs q about hidden causes x are from the correct ones. It is never smaller than surprise, and equals it when the beliefs are exact.
- `surprise.fep.intro1`: Karl Friston's free-energy principle says that a living system stays in the small set of states that keep it alive, and that it does this by minimising surprise: how unlikely its sensations are under its own model of the world. Surprise itself cannot be computed directly by the system, so the principle uses an upper bound on it, variational free energy, which can be computed.
- `surprise.fep.intro2`: Perception lowers free energy by changing beliefs. Action lowers it by changing the sensations. Learning lowers it over a longer time by changing the model. Active inference is the name for the action half: the agent chooses actions whose predicted outcomes have low expected free energy.
- `surprise.fep.label`: SURPRISE · THE FREE-ENERGY PRINCIPLE
- `surprise.fep.surprise`: Surprise is the negative log probability of an observation o under the model. Rare observations have high surprise.

- `surprise.modes.closer`: Which is closer to Friston. LEARNING with the body preferences held. In active inference the parameters of the generative model are learned by the same free-energy minimisation that drives perception and action, on a slower time scale, while the prior preferences over outcomes belong to the kind of creature the agent is and are not rewritten by experience. FIXED is the special case with a learning rate of zero. Letting the preferences learn is the version the principle warns about: an agent that learns to prefer whatever happens to it stops acting to change anything.
- `surprise.modes.fixed`: FIXED. The prior is set once and never changes. An enemy stays exactly as surprising the hundredth time as the first, so the agent reacts to every enemy the same way. Surprise drives action only.
- `surprise.modes.label`: SURPRISE · THE MODES
- `surprise.modes.learning`: LEARNING. After every step the model takes one Boltzmann learning step on what it saw. Views of enemies can become more expected, so the first sight of later enemies can become less surprising (habituation; the measured table shows how much). With the body preferences held (the default), habituation touches only what views look like; being hurt and being alarmed stay exactly as unwelcome. With the checkbox on, the preferences learn too, and the agent learns to expect being hurt and alarmed; the table measures what that does.
- `surprise.modes.title`: FIXED and LEARNING, and which is closer to Friston
